question: When machines were repeatedly predicted to replace translators and interpreters (1954, 1966, today), what actually happened to the human work, and which part stays with people and for how long?

issues.note: Hard cut from a close-up of the translation monitor to the library street while the narration asks its central question; the question text is shown over a picture that has nothing to do with it.

Jump from the 1954 computer demonstration room to the 1966 office while the narration says 'within a few years. In 1966,'. The two rooms look unrelated and nothing signals the time jump other than a caption.
The quote card dissolves into the office, then the shot cuts to a typewriter close-up. The 'results were thin' narration sits over a document close-up and a typewriter that do not show it.
Cuts from the monitor close-up to a remote-interpreter room while the narration says 'translation, the written word'. The picture shows a video interpreter, so the picture and narration do not match.
The 'cannot yet' quote from the 2025 monitor cuts straight to the 1966 document, with the narration 'the comparison we can make' covering the jump. The comparison is not set up visually.
Cuts abruptly from the modern office to the 1954 street at night. The lighting differs from the earlier dusk street shots, and the caption '1954: a few years' is the only link.
The courtroom booth view is held across several frames with almost no change in the picture.
The computer demonstration room is held across several frames and the shot barely changes.
The same dusk street with the lamp is shown for about 20 seconds in the closing section (R17.1 to R17.5), with little new to look at.
